title: Frame-Based Stereotactic Surgery for a Deep-Seated Brain Cavernoma: A Case Report and Technical Video
abstract: Abstract Background Cerebral cavernomas are the second most common vascular malformation of the central nervous system. While microsurgical excision is standard for accessible symptomatic lesions, stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is preferred for deep-seated or inaccessible cavernomas due to the higher complication risk of open resection, despite carrying its own risks of delayed hemorrhage and radiation-induced injury. Frame-based stereotactic surgical excision may combine the targeting precision of SRS with the immediate efficacy of surgical resection while avoiding radiation exposure. Case Presentation: A 25-year-old female presented with a history of headache, photophobia, blurred vision, and intermittent vomiting. Examination revealed left lateral gaze limitation and bilateral papilledema. MRI demonstrated a 15×20×24 mm intra-axial lesion in the left thalamic region extending to the left cerebral peduncle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus, initially favored as glioma. After endoscopic third ventriculostomy and an inconclusive endoscopic biopsy, stereotactic partial excision was performed using a novel 3D-printed stereotactic frame. Intraoperative findings and histopathology confirmed cavernoma rather than glioma. The procedure was uneventful, with no hemorrhage on postoperative imaging, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day two with an intact neurological examination. Conclusion Frame-based stereotactic surgical excision using this novel low-cost stereotactic system enabled safe, precise debulking of a deep-seated, rare thalamic-peduncular cavernoma, achieving diagnostic confirmation and symptomatic mass-effect reduction without complications. This approach may offer a viable alternative for deep, eloquently located cavernomas where open microsurgery carries excessive risk and SRS risks incomplete treatment and radiation side effects, warranting further evaluation in larger case series.

title: Early- Versus Late-Onset Fetal Growth Restriction: Clinical Features, Placental Histopathology, and Risk Factor Analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a critical adverse pregnancy complication that significantly contributes to adverse perinatal prognosis, and its clinical manifestations, pathological mechanisms and prognostic impacts vary greatly according to the gestational age of onset. Early-onset and late-onset FGR differ substantially in disease severity and underlying etiologies, to date, few studies have systematically compared the clinical characteristics and placental histopathological lesions of early- and late-onset FGR. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the clinical profiles and placental pathological changes between the two FGR subtypes and further screen key risk factors for early-onset FGR, so as to provide pathological and clinical evidence for the early identification and stratified clinical management of early-onset FGR. Methods Our cohort investigation encompassed 461 singleton pregnancies, including FGR, stratified by gestational age at diagnosis into early- and late-onset groups. Maternal demographics, pregnancy complications, delivery outcomes, Doppler parameters, and placental pathology were contrasted across groups. Multivariate regression characterized risk factors for early-onset FGR was constructed. Results Early-onset FGR was associated with significantly lower birth weight, higher preterm birth (PB) rates, worse perinatal outcomes, and more severe maternal vascular malperfusion (MVM) in placental lesions compared to late-onset FGR ( p < 0.05). Relevant risk factors associated with early-onset FGR included autoimmune disease, thyroid disorder, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), and abnormal umbilical artery Doppler, with a particularly strong association with preeclampsia. Conclusion Early-onset FGR is characterized by greater disease severity and is strongly linked to maternal systemic conditions, placental vascular insufficiency, and aberrant Doppler hemodynamics. Early-onset FGR is fundamentally a placenta-mediated vascular disorder, compounded by secondary inflammatory activation and maternal systemic dysfunction. Targeted management of these risk factors may improve perinatal outcomes.

title: Diagnosing Susac Syndrome Despite Incomplete Clinical Triad: A Case Report of Convergent Atypical Neuroimaging and Inflammatory Cerebrospinal Fluid Findings: Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Susac syndrome (SuS) is a rare autoimmune endotheliopathy involving the brain, retina, and inner ear. Because patients frequently present without the complete clinical triad of encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions (BRAO), and sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), diagnosis can be challenging. The European Susac Consortium (EuSaC) criteria classify SuS according to objective involvement of the brain, retinal, and vestibulocochlear domains; however, many patients do not fulfill criteria for probable or definite disease at initial presentation. Furthermore, neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings may overlap with inflammatory demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS). We report a case where EuSaC criteria was not met, however there was strong clinical and radiographic evidence to support the diagnosis of SuS. This case brings to question whether strict fulfillment of EuSaC criteria is needed to initiate early inpatient treatment to prevent irreversible neurological deficits. Case presentation We report the case of a woman in her early forties with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease, recurrent ischemic strokes, and an unspecified hypercoagulable disorder who presented with progressive gait instability, dizziness, and bilateral lower extremity weakness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated characteristic central corpus callosum “snowball” lesions and cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement. CSF analysis revealed elevated immunoglobulin G (IgG) index, elevated IgG synthesis rate, and markedly elevated myelin basic protein (MBP) in the absence of oligoclonal bands (OCB). At the time of presentation, only the brain domain of the EuSaC criteria was objectively fulfilled, and the patient therefore did not meet criteria for probable or definite SuS. Nevertheless, the characteristic neuroimaging phenotype, inflammatory CSF profile without oligoclonal bands, and absence of typical MS features strongly favored SuS and prompted treatment with high dose steroids and further diagnostic evaluation. Conclusions This case demonstrates that strict fulfillment of EuSaC criteria may not be required to recognize SuS when characteristic neuroradiographic findings and supportive clinical features are present. Recognition of central corpus callosum “snowball” lesions and cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement may facilitate earlier diagnosis and treatment, potentially reducing irreversible neurologic, retinal, and auditory morbidity.

title: Gelfoam-Induced Acute Cauda Equina Syndrome Following L3–L5 Decompression and Instrumented Fusion: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Absorbable gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) is a widely used hemostatic material in spinal surgery. Although generally safe, rare but devastating compressive neurological complications have been reported in intracranial, cervical, and thoracic procedures. Case presentation: A 71‑year‑old Chinese male underwent L3-L5 laminectomy, bilateral L3/4 and L4/5 foraminotomy, pedicle screw fixation, and cage implantation with autogenous bone graft for symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis. An intact sheet of Gelfoam was placed over the dura for hemostasis and left in situ at wound closure. Upon awakening from anesthesia two hours after surgery, the patient developed severe right lower extremity motor weakness, with muscle strength of 1/5 in the quadriceps, tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and extensor digitorum longus. On postoperative day 2, emergency lumbar spine CT revealed significant cauda equina compression at L4/5, prompting emergency surgical exploration and decompression. Intraoperatively, an expanded Gelfoam mass with adjacent clot was found circumferentially compressing the dural sac and cauda equina nerve roots from L3 to L5. The entire material was removed, and bilateral nerve root canals were further decompressed. Post‑decompression MRI confirmed complete relief of canal compromise. Muscle strength improved substantially, with all affected groups recovering to 3/5 except the extensor hallucis longus (2/5). Epidural drainage output was only 20 mL and 35 mL on the first two days after the second surgery, supporting that the compression was predominantly Gelfoam mass effect rather than an expanding hematoma. Conclusions : Placement of an intact, unprepared Gelfoam sheet in a closed epidural space can induce hyperacute cauda equina syndrome dominated by motor deficits within hours after surgery, a pattern distinctly different from the previously reported delayed onset of 10-14 days. Indwelling Foley catheterization may mask urinary retention, a classic autonomic warning sign, and delay early recognition. Strict adherence to standardized intraoperative protocols-soaking in thrombin, squeezing to expel air, using only small pieces, and removing residual material after hemostasis-is essential to prevent swelling‑induced mass effect. For patients presenting with severe unilateral lower extremity weakness immediately after surgery and no evidence of hardware misplacement on CT, urgent lumbar MRI and prompt decompression are recommended to maximize neurological recovery.

title: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Ophthalmic Foundation Models with Point-Based Classification and Retrieval
abstract: Abstract General-purpose vision foundation models have been evaluated across a wide range of tasks to demonstrate the versatility of their learned representations. By contrast, ophthalmic foundation models have largely been assessed using a narrow set of downstream tasks, primarily disease classification and segmentation, providing only a limited view of their representational capabilities. Considering how clinicians interpret ophthalmic images, where disease-relevant clinical signs are identified before diagnosis, we introduced an ophthalmic foundation model evaluation framework comprising two tasks: 1) point-supervised disease classification and 2) point-guided clinical sign-based image retrieval. Each task incorporates sparse point annotations indicating disease-relevant evidence locations. We applied this approach to diabetic retinopathy using colour fundus photography (CFP) and age-related macular degeneration using both CFP and optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans. Our evaluation spanned 11 foundation models across four newly curated and six established datasets. The results reveal that existing ophthalmic foundation models, despite their strong performance on disease classification, still struggle with the clinical sign retrieval task, although they outperform general-purpose foundation models. Our findings highlight the need to improve these models' capabilities at the fine-grained sign-level. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate further research on ophthalmic foundation models.

title: “Endoscopic Management of Advanced Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma with Extensive Infratemporal Fossa Extension: Surgical Challenges and Technical Modifications”- Case report
abstract: Abstract Background: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a rare, benign yet locally invasive vascular tumour affecting adolescent males. Advanced tumours extending into the infratemporal fossa (ITF) pose significant surgical challenges. Case Report: An 11-year-old boy presented with a one-year history of progressive left-sided proptosis and a two-month history of left cheek swelling. Imaging revealed a highly vascular mass centred in the left sphenopalatine fossa, extending into the infratemporal fossa, orbit, nasopharynx, cavernous sinus, and extradural temporal lobe. Preoperative embolisation was performed to reduce intraoperative blood loss. The tumour was completely excised via a transnasal endoscopic approach with few modifications. The postoperative course was uneventful, and follow-up imaging at two months demonstrated no residual disease. Histopathology confirmed JNA. Conclusion: This case demonstrates that exclusive endoscopic transnasal excision, combined with preoperative embolisation, can achieve complete resection of advanced JNA with extensive ITF extension, avoiding morbid open approaches.

title: Can simplified endoscopic score for Crohn’s disease be simpler? --Development and Validation of the Multimodal Activity Score for Crohn's Disease (MAS-CD)
abstract: Abstract Background Endoscopy is central to diagnosing and monitoring Crohn’s disease (CD), but current endoscopic scoring systems such as the Simplified Endoscopic Score for Crohn’s Disease (SES-CD) are complex, time-consuming, and limited when ileocolonoscopy is incomplete. Approximately 30–40% of CD patients cannot undergo full examinations, hindering comprehensive assessment. With mucosal healing now a key therapeutic target, there is an urgent need for a simpler, multimodal, and clinically practical scoring tool. Objectives To develop and prospectively validate a novel comprehensive assessment tool—the Multimodal Activity Score for Crohn’s Disease (MAS-CD)—that combines endoscopic and, when necessary, radiological parameters. Design: Multicenter development and prospective validation study. Methods Four parameters—ulcer size, ulcerated surface area, affected surface area, and stenosis severity—were scored on a 0–3 scale. For incomplete ileocolonoscopies, contrast-enhanced CT enterography (CTE) with optional magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) or intestinal ultrasound (IUS) were incorporated. Inter-rater reproducibility was assessed in 157 patients, and MAS-CD was developed using multivariable regression. Validation was conducted in an independent cohort of 91 patients. Correlations with SES-CD, Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI), serum C-reactive protein (CRP), albumin, and fecal calprotectin were analyzed. Results Interobserver agreement for MAS-CD parameters was substantial (Kappa 0.508–0.722; ICC = 0.888). MAS-CD strongly correlated with SES-CD (r = 0.816, p < 0.001) and showed significant associations with CRP (r = 0.28), HBI (r = 0.285), albumin (r=–0.208), and fecal calprotectin (r = 0.218) (all p < 0.05). MAS-CD differentiated remission from active disease, small bowel-from colonic-dominant phenotypes, and predicted treatment response more effectively than SES-CD (AUC 0.61 vs. 0.21, p < 0.05). Conclusion MAS-CD is a simplified, flexible, and reproducible multimodal scoring system that overcomes the limitations of incomplete endoscopic assessment. By integrating imaging data, it provides a clinically actionable tool for comprehensive disease activity monitoring and treat-to-target strategies in the biologic era.

title: Parasagittal High-Convexity Tightness Reveals a Focal Site of CSF Outflow Impairment in Ventriculomegaly
abstract: Abstract Introduction Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) and resistance to CSF outflow (R out ) are two of the most consistent diagnostic and prognostic markers in normal pressure hydrocephalus, yet it remains unclear whether they reflect a common pathophysiological process. A plausible link is that tightness of the high convexities adjacent to the superior sagittal sinus (SSS), the principal CSF outflow region, compromises CSF drainage and thereby increases R out . To test this hypothesis, we investigated the association between parasagittal high-convexity CSF volume near the SSS and R out in subjects undergoing MRI and CSF infusion testing. Methods We conducted a retrospective study of 621 individuals (581 with ventriculomegaly and 40 without), investigated with CSF infusion testing and brain MRI. Parasagittal high convexity CSF volumes were quantified using a semi-automated segmentation approach, focusing on anatomically defined high convexity regions. R out was derived from lumbar CSF infusion testing using standardised protocols. Associations between parasagittal CSF volume and R out were evaluated using correlation analyses, with additional assessment of demographic and structural confounders. Results An inverse relationship was observed between parasagittal high convexity CSF volume and R out (N = 621, Spearman Rho =-0.42, p < 0.001). This association was most pronounced when measurements were restricted to anatomically localised regions adjacent to the SSS, while more extended convexity regions demonstrated weaker relationships (N = 309, Rho=-0.14, p = 0.0002). The observed association was preserved after exclusion of healthy individuals. Age, sex, and ventricular volume did not significantly influence the relationship. Conclusions A localised relationship exists between parasagittal high-convexity morphology and resistance to CSF outflow. The regional specificity of this association suggests that DESH and R out may reflect a shared pathophysiological mechanism, which becomes apparent only when examined at anatomically strategic sites along the CSF outflow pathway.

title: Dual-encoder cross-scale dependency fusion network for placenta segmentation using MR and ultrasound images
abstract: Abstract Accurate placenta segmentation is essential for prenatal assessment, pregnancy management, and the diagnosis of placenta-related abnormalities. However, automatic placenta segmentation remains challenging due to complex anatomical structures, ambiguous boundaries, intensity variations, and substantial differences between imaging modalities. In this study, we propose a dual-encoder cross-scale dependency fusion network (DECSDF-Net) for placenta segmentation using MR and ultrasound images. The proposed DECSDF-Net adopts a dual-encoder architecture to extract complementary hierarchical features from two parallel encoding pathways. To enhance spatial representation, a cross-directional coordinate attention module (CDCAM) is introduced to capture directional dependencies and strengthen boundary-related features. Furthermore, a guided cross-scale dependency module (GCSDM) is designed to establish adaptive interactions among multi-level features, enabling effective information exchange between low-level spatial details and high-level semantic representations. An attention-guided enhanced receptive field block (AGERFB) is developed to improve contextual feature extraction by integrating multi-scale receptive fields with attention refinement. In addition, a progressive multi-scale feature fusion module (PMSFFM) is incorporated into the decoder to progressively aggregate features from different resolutions and enhance segmentation accuracy. To validate the effectiveness of DECSDF-Net, two placenta segmentation databases, namely Placenta-MR and Placenta-US, were constructed from magnetic resonance and ultrasound images. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, DECSDF-Net achieved superior segmentation performance on both datasets. title: Evaluation Metrics for Image Classification, Segmentation and Localization
abstract: Abstract Evaluation metrics dictate the incentives for an image analysis system, detect remaining failures, and verify any proposed improvement in scientific or clinical claims. Despite the mathematical similarity of classification, segmentation, and localization, the units, matching criteria, and practice implications vary across these tasks. The current review analyzes the distinctions through the lens of a selected sample of 150 bibliographically validated references, including 10 papers from the provided author profile. It incorporates foundational statistics, state-of-the-art benchmarking practices, medical imaging use cases, and recent developments in uncertainties, selective prediction, and deployment. The review organizes 72 metrics and corresponding evaluation quantities by the question they answer: correctness of decision, score discrimination, reliability of probabilities, spatial correspondence, recovery of objects, localization of geometry, or practical utility. Comparisons describe equations, assumptions, aggregation approaches, advantages, and failures. Ten deterministic worked examples demonstrate prevalence effects, constant discrimination and worsening probability scores, reverse rankings because of aggregation, hidden border failures by overlap, detection matching, physical landmark errors, and the cost of abstaining. Twenty-four numeric instances from 4 separate publications supply additional citations and examples without pooling the inconsistent results. The primary takeaway is that a sound evaluation requires a small and preselected set of metrics, complementary to each other, applicable to the defined population, unit, reference standard, and decision. For classification, operating point performance is always required, along with discrimination and probability metrics. Segmentation demands appropriate measures of overlap, borders, and object topology. Localization needs explicitly stated criteria of correspondence and tolerance and false positive control. Independent partitioning, uncertainties, subgroups, and workflow outputs determine the interpretability of the metrics. This manuscript is an organized critical review and methodology resource, but not a completed systematic review according to PRISMA criteria, meta-analysis, or benchmark of a new model. The attached list of metrics, reference export, extraction notes, computational code, and reporting checklist help design and validate reproducible studies and author reviews.

title: Brain Tumor Segmentation in the Foundation-Model
abstract: Abstract Automated brain tumor segmentation has progressed from handcrafted pipelines and U-Net variants to self-configuring 3D CNNs, transformer hybrids, state-space models, diffusion based segmenters, promptable models and brain-specific foundation models. Yet the field’s central scientific problem has changed: another fractional gain in Dice on a familiar BraTS split provides limited evidence that a system will remain reliable when MRI sequences are missing, scanners and institutions change, lesions are small or multifocal, postoperative anatomy is distorted, or uncertainty is high. This structured critical review synthesizes 150 references with emphasis on 2025–2026 and compares architectures, multimodal fusion strategies, preprocessing, missing-modality learning, self-supervision, foundation-model adaptation, federated learning, domain adaptation, uncertainty quantification and clinical translation. We organize evidence around adult glioma, pediatric tumors, brain metastases, meningioma and longitudinal/postoperative applications; distinguish region overlap from lesion detection and volumetric clinical endpoints; and critically examine leakage, site confounding, hidden test reuse, pretraining contamination, annotation uncertainty and challenge-overfitting. Recent evidence is especially informative: brain MRI foundation models such as BrainIAC and BrainFound improve label efficiency and cross-task transfer, while task specific systems such as nnU-Net and carefully engineered 2.5D/3D networks remain formidable full-data baselines. Missing-modality studies increasingly favor adaptive fusion, distillation and modality dropout over naive zero-filling; uncertainty work is moving toward conformal and evidential approaches that can identify cases requiring expert review; and external studies of metastases and meningiomas demonstrate why lesion-wise, site-stratified and human-in-the-loop evaluation is essential. We propose DATA-SEG, Dataset, Annotation, Train/test integrity, Architecture, Statistics, External robustness and Governance, as a reporting and evaluation framework. The review concludes that the next high-impact phase of brain tumor segmentation should prioritize post-cutoff hidden benchmarks, cross-site robustness, missing-sequence stress tests, calibrated selective segmentation, multi-rater probabilistic ground truth and longitudinal clinical readouts rather than leaderboard optimization alone.

title: HLNet: High-Confidence Lightweight Network for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Semi-Supervised Learning(SSL) can effectively alleviate the reliance on large amounts of pixel-level labeled data when training fully supervised medical image segmentation models. However, most current semi-supervised learning approaches rely on self-training or consistency regularization methods, which are highly susceptible to erroneous supervision from low-quality pseudo-labels, thus affecting model segmentation performance. Additionally, existing semi-supervised backbone networks typically have large parameter sizes, making them unsuitable for portable device designs. To address these issues, this paper proposes a lightweight semi-supervised segmentation model with high confidence under dual-level perturbations. Perturbations are applied at both the input data and model levels to guide the model in learning more robust feature representations. Furthermore, low-quality pixels are ignored, and EVidence Inference Learning(EVIL) is introduced to estimate the uncertainty of pseudo-labels, mitigating the erroneous supervision from pseudo-labels during training. Experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms comparison models on three different public datasets—ACDC, BUSI, and Promise12. With only 20% labeled data, the model achieves promising segmentation performance in terms of Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Jaccard index, while significantly reducing the number of parameters.

title: Thalamic Tuberculoma Presenting as Isolated Gait Disturbance Without Systemic or Meningeal Symptoms in a 2-Year-Old Child: A Case Report.
abstract: Intracranial tuberculoma is an important manifestation of pediatric central nervous system tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions. While seizures and signs of raised intracranial pressure are common presenting features, isolated focal neurological deficits without systemic or meningeal symptoms are rare, resulting in diagnostic delay. We report an unusual case of thalamic tuberculoma presenting primarily with gait disturbance in a young child. A 2-year-old boy from Karachi, Pakistan, presented with inability to walk independently at 20 months age. On neurological examination, he had decreased power involving left side of body. MRI of the brain showed a ring-enhancing lesion in the right thalamus extending into the midbrain with surrounding vasogenic edema. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) showed a lipid/lactate peak, which supported an infectious granulomatous etiology; a presumptive diagnosis of tuberculoma was made based on imaging findings and household TB exposure. Although intracranial tuberculoma does not always present with systemic manifestations of tuberculosis in children, as observed in the present study, it is also a challenging disease to diagnose in young children due to the atypical presentation. Neuroimaging: Early diagnosis is possible. For deep-seated lesions where operative therapy and surgical treatment are highly risky, conservative management is often effective with anti-tuberculous therapy and adjunctive corticosteroids. Early physiotherapy to achieve functional recovery is very important. The case illustrates the need for consideration of intracranial tuberculoma in an individual neurological impairment case, considering children with isolated neurological deficits, when systemic forms of tuberculosis do not develop, even in the absence of evidence of systemic tuberculosis symptoms and history of direct exposure. Prompt imaging, early diagnosis, and treatment with anti-tuberculous therapy may lead to good outcomes.

title: Pyogenic Granuloma in the Sinonasal Cavity: A Potential 38-Year Latency Following Foreign Body Entrapment.
abstract: Lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH), also known as pyogenic granuloma (PG), is a benign vascular lesion typically associated with minor trauma or irritation, predominantly occurring in the oral cavity and in females. Its sinonasal occurrence, particularly in males, is rare, and an association with remote childhood trauma remains a speculative hypothesis. Clinically, it must be differentiated from other vascular sinonasal lesions such as angiofibroma, hemangioma variants, and malignant mimics. This rare case report descripts a highly unusual case of an inflammatory nasal mass in a 43-year-old male who presented with left-sided nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and hyposmia for two months. Endoscopic evaluation and CT/MRI revealed a highly vascular mass attached to the left middle turbinate. Notably, the patient had a history of foreign body entrapment in the left nasal cavity at the age of 5, which was removed without immediate complications. This suggests a potential association between the initial trauma and the subsequent manifestation of the lesion after a 38-year latency period. The mass was successfully excised en bloc through endoscopic surgery. This case highlights a potential, albeit rare, etiological association for sinonasal PG, raising the hypothesis that past mucosal trauma, such as a foreign body, may contribute to the delayed formation of vascular lesions decades later, particularly in a male patient at an unusual nasal site. A comprehensive diagnostic workup, including imaging and histopathology, is essential to confirm the diagnosis and ensure complete surgical management. The patient remained asymptomatic with no recurrence observed at one-year follow-up.

title: Radiomics Model Based on Gd-DTPA-enhanced Multiparametric MRI Supports Noninvasive Pretreatment Prediction of Immunoscore in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Introduction This study assessed whether Gd-DTPA-enhanced MRI could predict the immunoscore in HCC noninvasively before therapy, without the need for tissue sampling. Methods Retrospectively, surgically treated HCC patients who had a preoperative Gd-DTPA-enhanced MRI exam were enrolled. Eligible patients were randomly allocated to a training set and a validation set following a 3:1 randomization scheme. Immunohistochemistry was performed to quantify CD3-positive and CD8-positive cell densities; patients were stratified into high and low immunoscore groups using the median cutoff. Volumes of interest encompassing hepatic lesions, including intratumoral and peritumoral 10-mm margins, were manually delineated on multiparametric MRI sequences for radiomics feature extraction. Clinical and pathological data were retrieved from electronic medical records. A Support Vector Machine (SVM) was used to develop three predictive models: (1) Intratumoral Radiomics Model (IRM), (2) combined intra- and peritumoral radiomics model (CRM), and (3) Clinical Combined Radiomics Model (CCRM). Model performance was compared using the DeLong test and evaluated via the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). Results Of 111 eligible patients, 83 were assigned to the training cohort and 28 to the validation cohort. Baseline characteristics were balanced between cohorts. The CCRM demonstrated the highest AUC values in both cohorts (training: 0.947; validation: 0.913). Compared with IRM, CCRM showed significantly better performance in the validation cohort (p = 0.016) but not in the training cohort (p = 0.084). In the validation cohort, CCRM did not significantly outperform CRM (p = 0.55), whereas a significant difference was observed in the training cohort (p = 0.036). Calibration curves demonstrated good agreement. DCA indicated that the CCRM and the CRM achieved similar overall net benefits, which were higher than those of the IRM across threshold probabilities of 46% to 98%. Discussion This radiomics approach suggests the feasibility of using routine Gd-DTPA-enhanced MRI for preoperative immunoscore prediction in HCC, providing preliminary evidence for tumor immune characterization. Conclusion A radiomics model integrating intra- and peritumoral MRI features enables noninvasive preoperative immunoscore prediction in HCC, which may provide preliminary support for individualized immunotherapy decision-making, although external validation is warranted.

title: Ocular Factors Affecting AI Diagnosis in Diabetic Retinopathy Screening for Resource-Limited Regions: Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of vision loss among working-age adults worldwide. AI-assisted automated image reading has effectively alleviated the human resource challenges in large-scale remote screenings, yet there is limited analysis on the impact of complex ocular factors on the diagnostic efficacy of AI. Objective This study aimed to systematically analyze the impact of multiple ocular factors on the diagnostic efficacy of the EVisionAI system in detecting DR and vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy (VTDR) during large-scale screening of residents with diabetes in resource-limited regions. Methods This cross-sectional study used a multistage stratified random sampling method to screen residents with type 2 diabetes at primary health centers in resource-limited regions. Data collection involved structured questionnaires (for basic and disease information), hemoglobin A 1c testing, and comprehensive ophthalmic examinations (visual acuity, intraocular pressure, slit-lamp examination, axial length measurement, and fundus photography). Following data collection, 2 ophthalmologists independently graded fundus photographs according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology standards. The influence of various ocular factors on the diagnostic performance of EVisionAI was subsequently evaluated. Results Between October 21 and November 12, 2024, 1847 participants with type 2 diabetes (aged 32-91 years) were enrolled, of whom 1748 (94.6%) completed the screening process and 3392 eyes were eligible for DR analysis. Participants had a mean age of 67.17 (SD 8.52) years and mean diabetes duration of 9.13 (SD 6.97) years, with 19.2% (335/1748) having DR and 7.4% (129/1748) having VTDR. Although EVisionAI's diagnostic efficacy was comparable to that of ophthalmologists (sensitivity: 90.61%, 95% CI 87.89%-92.79%; specificity: 98.99%, 95% CI 98.52%-99.31%), some ocular factors-including pupil size, refractive media opacity, and tessellated fundus (TF)-significantly impaired its efficiency. Severe refractive media opacity and TF reduced its sensitivity to 80.95% and 82.86%, respectively, and these factors interfered more with early-stage DR detection than VTDR (97.45% detected), particularly in eyes with severe TF changes (sensitivity decreased to 60.71%). Most notably, severe vitreous degeneration-induced opacity almost invariably led to VTDR misdiagnosis. Additionally, pupil dilation improved the sensitivity of EVisionAI for diagnosing DR (excluding early-stage DR) but had minimal impact on specificity. Conclusions EVisionAI achieved high diagnostic accuracy for large-scale DR screening in resource-limited regions, yet its performance for early-stage disease was diminished by severe ocular factors. Optimizing for these factors is therefore essential to maximize its clinical utility in primary care settings with limited specialist access.

Severe refractive media opacity and TF reduced its sensitivity to 80.95% and 82.86%, respectively, and these factors interfered more with early-stage DR detection than VTDR (97.45% detected), particularly in eyes with severe TF changes (sensitivity decreased to 60.71%). Most notably, severe vitreous degeneration-induced opacity almost invariably led to VTDR misdiagnosis. Additionally, pupil dilation improved the sensitivity of EVisionAI for diagnosing DR (excluding early-stage DR) but had minimal impact on specificity.

Conclusions

EVisionAI achieved high diagnostic accuracy for large-scale DR screening in resource-limited regions, yet its performance for early-stage disease was diminished by severe ocular factors. Optimizing for these factors is therefore essential to maximize its clinical utility in primary care settings with limited specialist access.

title: MRI Evaluation and Reporting in Suspected and Established Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus, AJR Expert Panel Review.
abstract: This AJR Expert Panel Narrative Review summarizes MRI features of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) and their utility in various clinical scenarios, describes imaging features suggestive of alternate or co-pathology, and provides a framework for reporting such findings. iNPH is characterized by gait impairment, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence that may be improved with CSF shunting. Imaging is an important part of the diagnostic assessment for iNPH by identifying findings supportive of a diagnosis of iNPH or of alternate diagnoses or co-pathology. Although MRI features of iNPH have been proposed, these features' utility for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring have varied among studies. The imaging assessment for suspected iNPH should include an unenhanced brain MRI examination incorporating, among other sequences, a 3D-T1weighted sequence. Key imaging features supportive of an iNPH diagnosis include: ventriculomegaly, high-convexity narrowed sulci, and enlarged Sylvian fissures (collectively termed disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus [DESH]), along with cerebral aqueduct patency. Incidentally detected findings of iNPH may be summarized in the report impression as "findings supportive of a diagnosis of iNPH in the appropriate clinical context." This article concludes with consensus statements summarizing MRI protocols and findings to report in the diagnostic assessment and treatment monitoring of iNPH.

title: Nasopharyngeal and laryngopharyngeal collapse: intra- and interrater agreement supports novel endoscopic scoring classifications in horses.
abstract: Objective The contribution of reduced airway patency from heightened inspiratory pressure or active muscular contraction to the pathophysiology of pharyngeal collapse is unknown. Existing classifications refer to the entire pharyngeal region; however, anatomical differences are evident between rostral and caudal collapse. Novel classifications and grading systems are proposed to differentiate 2 pathologies: nasopharyngeal collapse (NPC; collapse of ≥ 1 pharyngeal wall rostral to the tip of the epiglottis; grades 0 through 4), and laryngopharyngeal collapse (LPC; collapse of ≥ 1 pharyngeal wall caudal to the tip of the epiglottis; grades 0 through 3). Methods Clinical reports from 99 barrel racing horses in Southern Alberta previously diagnosed with pharyngeal collapse via overground endoscopy (2015 through 2025) were retrospectively analyzed. Horses were referred for respiratory signs and/or poor performance. Two raters independently assessed still images obtained during high-speed exercise in a blinded and randomized fashion. Descriptive statistics and intrarater/interrater agreement for classification (McNemar test) and scoring (weighted κ) were reported. Results Similar frequencies of NPC (64.6%) and LPC (67.6%) were observed (32% had both). Intrarater agreement for NPC was χ2 = 7.0 (rater 1) and χ2 = 1.0 (rater 2) for NPC and χ2 = 2.0 (rater 1) and χ2 = 1.6 (rater 2) for LPC. Scoring agreement was good to very good for NPC (κ = 0.69 to 0.81) and moderate to good for LPC (κ = 0.56 to 0.80), indicating reliable performance. Interrater agreement was χ2 = 4.6 (rater 1) and χ2 = 0.7 (rater 2) for NPC and χ2 = 0.2 (rater 1) and 2.0 (rater 2) for LPC. Conclusions Intra- and interrater agreement supports the feasibility and practicality of distinguishing NPC from LPC. Clinical relevance Novel classifications reflecting functional anatomy may provide insight into the pathophysiology of pharyngeal collapse.

title: Head-to-Head Comparison of Neuroblastoma Detection by [ 64 Cu]GD2 PET and [ 123 I]MIBG SPECT.
abstract: 123 I-labeled metaiodobenzylguanidine ([ 123 I]MIBG) SPECT is well-established for neuroblastoma diagnostics. Nevertheless, therapies targeting GD2 on neuroblastoma gain clinical importance in standard treatment and clinical trials, which emphasizes the relevance of PET using the radiolabeled GD2 antibody [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-ch14.18/CHO ([ 64 Cu]GD2) for noninvasive detection of GD2 expression. Here, we present an initial comparison of the diagnostic performance of [ 64 Cu]GD2 PET and [ 123 I]MIBG SPECT. Methods: Five patients with neuroblastoma underwent [ 123 I]MIBG SPECT, [ 64 Cu]GD2 PET, and MRI. The detected lesions were compared between [ 123 I]MIBG and [ 64 Cu]GD2 using International Society of Pediatric Oncology Europe Neuroblastoma (SIOPEN) and modified Curie scores. Results: Three patients suffered from multiple metastases, and 2 patients presented solitary lymph node metastases. Both modalities detected lesions in every patient; [ 64 Cu]GD2 revealed additional lesions in patients with multiple metastases compared with [ 123 I]MIBG, leading to higher SIOPEN and modified Curie scores. Conclusion: These initial data indicate the diagnostic suitability of [ 64 Cu]GD2 for detection of neuroblastoma metastasis.

title: Fully Automated Segmentation of [ 18 F]FDG and [ 68 Ga]/[ 18 F]PSMA PET/CT Images via Data-Centric Deep Learning.
abstract: The purpose of this study was to develop and validate lesion identification in oncologic nuclear imaging (LION), an open-source PET-only tumor segmentation pipeline for [ 18 F]FDG and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted PET/CT, and to investigate how training data characteristics influence segmentation performance. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter study, 5209 [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT scans spanning 19 disease types and 2046 PSMA-targeted PET/CT scans were used to train PET-only segmentation models. Tumor segmentation incorporated organs with physiologic uptake as auxiliary classes to enable PET-only inference. Tumor occurrence maps (TOMs) quantified tumor spatial diversity across the training data. For [ 18 F]FDG, disease-specific and mixed-disease models trained on progressively larger subsets were compared to test whether increasing spatial diversity improves generalization. Scanner-related domain shift was analyzed using DINOv2 embeddings. Models were evaluated on multicenter holdout cohorts (616 [ 18 F]FDG scans across 4 diseases; 443 PSMA-targeted prostate cancer scans) and compared with 3 open-source tools. Results: Organ context improved median Dice from 0.62 to 0.71 for [ 18 F]FDG and from 0.75 to 0.83 for PSMA, on the complete holdout cohorts. Spatial diversity measured by TOMs was strongly associated with Dice (Spearman ρ = 0.80, P = 0.003). A mixed-disease model trained on 500 patients matched the performance of a lymphoma specialist model trained on 3031 cases. DINOv2 embeddings revealed scanner-induced domain shift between same-disease cohorts. LION achieved median Dice scores of 0.71 for [ 18 F]FDG and 0.85 for PSMA and outperformed other open-source approaches on the model-comparison test set, which excluded the AutoPET test cases. Conclusion: LION enables PET-only automated segmentation for [ 18 F]FDG and PSMA-targeted PET. Training data composition, particularly spatial diversity quantified by TOMs, was strongly associated with segmentation performance.

title: PSYCHIATRY The Case for Starting Over
abstract: AbstractPsychiatry is the only branch of medicine that still diagnoses without reference to the organ it treats. Psychiatry: The Case for Starting Over argues that this is a structural failure rather than a temporary gap. The descriptive nosology inherited from Kraepelin and formalized in the DSM achieved diagnostic reliability at the cost of validity. Its categories were assembled by committee consensus rather than grounded in mechanism, and so it cannot guide the circuit-targeted therapies now reshaping the field.The book traces this problem historically and then builds an alternative from three converging lines of work. The first is computational neural-network modeling of psychopathology, from Hopfield and Hinton through Hoffman's simulations of schizophrenia and the author's own work. The second is systems neuroscience, including large-scale networks, global workspace and integrated information theories, attractor dynamics, and small-world connectivity. The third is Friston's Free Energy Principle and predictive processing.From this synthesis the book introduces Neuroanalysis and its clinical instrument, Clinical Brain Profiling (CBP). CBP treats mental disorders as disturbances of dynamic brain-network organization and organizes them across four timescales of plasticity:•Cognizance plasticity (milliseconds) is centered on the central executive network and linked to psychosis and negative signs.•Reactive plasticity (minutes to hours) is centered on the salience network and linked to anxiety.•Adaptive plasticity (days to weeks) sits at the salience–default mode interface and is linked to depression and mania.•Developmental plasticity (lifetime) is centered on the default mode network and linked to personality disorder patterns.The book reviews the neuromodulation toolkit: ECT, DBS, TMS, tDCS/tACS, psychedelic-assisted therapy, and focused ultrasound. It then proposes an entity-matched "grammar of plasticity" for selecting, combining, and sequencing these interventions. Guiding principles include strengthening prefrontal regulation before driving motivation, opening plasticity windows before directing them, and continuous biomarker monitoring.Throughout, the author separates established science from theoretical proposal and untested hypothesis. He outlines what validation would require: prospective outcome trials, clinically feasible network measures, and a cultural shift from single-label diagnosis to multidimensional profiling. The result is a case for rebuilding psychiatry as a measurement-based, mechanism-guided clinical neuroscience.

title: FRESH-bioprinted vascular constructs: a quantitatively characterized workflow for reproducible device-oriented applications.
abstract: The lack of standardized and reproducible in vitro vascular models remains a major obstacle to the quantitative evaluation of endovascular devices and vessel-device interactions. While recent bioprinted vascular constructs have increased biological complexity, reproducibility, shape fidelity, and mechanical consistency remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we establish a quantitatively characterized FRESH-bioprinted workflow that enables reproducible fabrication and standardized characterization of vessel-like constructs for device-oriented testing. Bioink formulation, printing parameters, and post-processing conditions were systematically optimized. At the same time, construct geometry and mechanical reproducibility were quantitatively evaluated using micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), confined compression, and ring tensile testing. Sterile fabrication, preliminary cellularization, controlled perfusion, and intraluminal stent-like ring deployment were further explored to assess procedural compatibility within a device-oriented vascular testing framework. The optimized workflow enabled reproducible fabrication of vessel-like constructs across multiple geometrical scales, with close agreement between designed and measured dimensions and limited batch-to-batch variability. Micro-CT analysis revealed controlled post-processing-induced geometrical changes, including mild shrinkage and lumen reduction, while mechanical testing demonstrated reproducible axial and circumferential responses across independent fabrication batches. Intraluminal deployment of a radiopaque polycaprolactone ring induced local vessel expansion of approximately 8% while preserving lumen patency and structural integrity under low-pressure perfusion conditions. Preliminary biological assays confirmed high cell viability for up to 14 days and initial endothelial adhesion, supporting compatibility with sterile cell culture procedures and providing a robust foundation for future biologically advanced vascular models. By integrating biofabrication, quantitative imaging, mechanical characterization, and preliminary biological validation into a single workflow, this work establishes a quantitatively characterized and reproducible FRESH-bioprinted vascular platform that bridges the gap between rigid vascular phantoms and biologically advanced tissue-engineered systems. The proposed platform provides a robust experimental foundation for future process standardization, device-oriented vascular testing, and the progressive development of standardized experimental models for endovascular research.

title: Case Report: An enlarging left ventricular mass during anticoagulation in a patient receiving almonertinib after thoracic radiotherapy: diagnostic uncertainty and individualized management.
abstract: Distinguishing a left ventricular thrombus from a cardiac tumor is challenging when a large mass arises at an atypical non-apical site, particularly in a patient with cancer. We describe a 37-year-old man with epidermal growth factor receptor-mutant non-small cell lung cancer receiving almonertinib who developed a broad-based posterior wall left ventricular mass while cancer imaging remained stable. At detection, the reported left ventricular ejection fraction estimate was 55%, and no regional wall motion abnormality was documented. Cardiac CT showed no calcification or appreciable arterial- or delayed-phase enhancement, and Doppler echocardiography showed no internal flow. Low-mechanical-index contrast-enhanced echocardiography showed no appreciable internal perfusion in the contemporaneous examination report; later archived images also showed persistent absence of perfusion, although early-phase cine loops were not retained for retrospective reassessment. These concordant avascular features supported the presence of a thrombus but were not diagnostic. Cardiac magnetic resonance was recommended but declined because of financial concerns, and histopathology was unavailable. After approximately 9 months of prescribed edoxaban 60 mg once daily with reported adherence, the maximum linear dimension increased from 39.7 to 51.0 mm. A posterior wall regional wall motion abnormality was first documented 5 months after mass detection and therefore could not explain the lesion already present at detection. Edoxaban levels and edoxaban-calibrated anti-factor Xa activity were not measured, and human interaction data for almonertinib and edoxaban were unavailable. This case highlights the need to keep the diagnosis qualified and to reassess alternative pathology and anticoagulant exposure when an imaging-supported left ventricular thrombus follows an unexpected course.

title: A novel morphological assessment approach for abdominal aortic aneurysms: automated segmentation and measurement using a semi-supervised deep learning algorithm.
abstract: Background Morphological assessment of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is crucial for preoperative strategy formulation, but traditional manual assessment is time-consuming and subjective. Objectives This study aims to develop a novel semi-supervised deep learning (DL) framework for the automatic and accurate segmentation and measurement of AAA. Methods In this study, a semi-supervised learning algorithm was developed based on computed tomography angiography scans collected retrospectively from 88 AAA patients. The algorithm employed 16 labeled cases for supervised training and incorporated 47 unlabeled cases through consistency regularization to achieve accurate segmentation of the AAA lumen, aneurysm neck, and iliac arteries. To evaluate the model's segmentation performance, the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95) were utilized, and the agreement between automatically derived measurements and manual annotations was assessed. Results Among the models evaluated, Swin-UNETR achieved the best segmentation performance with 97.3% accuracy. The DSC was 0.965 ± 0.025 and 0.931 ± 0.021, and HD95 was 2.01 ± 0.39 mm and 2.93 ± 0.28 mm in the internal and independent test sets, respectively. Automation and expert measurements showed generally good-to-excellent agreement based on intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) analysis. In addition, average time per case decreased from 53.08 ± 8.17 to 4.18 ± 0.90 min, mouse movement distance from 91.62 ± 9.95 to 13.03 ± 3.12 m, and clicks from 672.62 ± 129.47 to 157.69 ± 0.90 times (all P < 0.001). Conclusions The proposed Swin-UNETR algorithm enables fast, reliable, and reproducible automated segmentation and measurement of key anatomical details of AAA.

title: Primary left ventricular intimal sarcoma: a case report of multimodality imaging and molecular confirmation.
abstract: Primary cardiac intimal sarcoma is a rare malignant mesenchymal neoplasm whose intracavitary appearance may mimic other cardiac masses. We report a woman in her early 60s with recurrent palpitations and occasional exertional dyspnea. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrated a giant, highly mobile, irregular multilobulated mass occupying most of the left ventricular cavity, with slit-like interlobular clefts and a probable broad-based attachment near the apical interventricular septum. Low-velocity color Doppler demonstrated residual flow around and between lobules, while continuous-wave Doppler showed a peak left ventricular outflow tract velocity of 3.09 m/s and a peak instantaneous gradient of 38 mmHg. Cardiac computed tomography angiography (CTA) showed a large relatively hypoattenuating left ventricular mass with heterogeneous enhancement: some portions showed no obvious enhancement, whereas others showed mild enhancement; the interface with the ventricular wall was locally indistinct, so myocardial involvement could not be excluded. After induction of general anesthesia, intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed the mass nearly filling the left ventricular cavity, but the attachment and fine multilobulated architecture were less clearly seen than on preoperative TTE. The patient underwent tumor resection with concomitant mitral valve repair. Histology showed mildly atypical spindle cells with fascicular and focal perivascular growth, readily identified mitotic figures, and mild myxoid stromal change. Immunohistochemistry showed MDM2 positivity, and fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrated MDM2 and CDK4 amplification, supporting the diagnosis of intimal sarcoma. At approximately 2 weeks after surgery, follow-up TTE showed no residual or recurrent left ventricular mass, preserved left ventricular systolic function, minimal residual mitral regurgitation, and a peak outflow tract velocity of 0.92 m/s without residual obstruction. Postoperative 18F-FDG PET/CT performed at approximately the same time identified no definite extracardiac primary tumor or obvious distant metastatic lesions. The case illustrates how multimodality imaging can define the anatomy and hemodynamic effects of a rare left ventricular intimal sarcoma, while histopathologic and molecular findings remain essential for definitive diagnosis.

title: Radiomics-Based prediction of renal prognosis in ANCA-associated vasculitis.
abstract: Objective To develop and validate a non-invasive prediction model combining renal CT radiomics features and clinical markers for assessing long-term renal prognosis at 1, 3, and 5 years in patients with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV). Methods A retrospective cohort of 262 AAV patients from Peking Union Medical College Hospital (2015-2020) was analyzed. Radiomics features (morphological, first-order, and texture) were extracted from segmented renal parenchyma on abdominopelvic CT. Clinical markers included demographics, serum creatinine, complement component 3 (C3), and other laboratory indicators. Renal volume, serum creatinine, and complement component 3 (C3) were pre-specified as predictors based on a priori biological rationale, and XGBoost was employed for model construction. Performance was evaluated via ROC-AUC (receiver operating characteristic/area under the curve), F1 score, decision curve analysis, and calibration curves. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis assessed feature contributions, and Kaplan-Meier curves with Bonferroni-corrected log-rank tests were used for survival stratification. Results The mean follow-up was 40.8 months; 59 patients (23%) developed ESRD (56 within 3 years) and 29 (11%) died. The combined model (renal volume + sCr + C3) achieved an AUC of 0.93 for 3-year ESRD prediction (clinical-only model: 0.91), with renal volume independently associated with ESRD (Wald p = 0.004). For the 3-year composite outcome, the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.84 (clinical-only: 0.81) with significantly improved reclassification (IDI p = 0.018; category-free NRI p = 0.024). In pre-specified median-based Kaplan-Meier analyses, reduced renal volume (≤ 130.6 mL), elevated serum creatinine (> 177.5 μmol/L) and lower C3 (≤ 0.97 g/L) were associated with poorer 3-year ESRD-free survival (log-rank p ≤ 0.002). Conclusion The integrated radiomics-clinical model provides accurate, non-invasive risk stratification for long-term renal outcomes in AAV, facilitating personalized treatment.

title: Prediction of early postoperative hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma: dual-outcome prediction models.
abstract: Background Postoperative hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism are two common complications after total or subtotal/near-total for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). This study aimed to identify significant predictors of early postoperative hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism and develop prediction nomograms for risk stratification in PTC patients. Methods A total of 1036 PTC patients who underwent total or subtotal/near-total thyroidectomy were retrospectively enrolled. Multivariable logistic regression with prespecified variables was performed to identify independent predictors for two outcomes: (1) early postoperative hypocalcemia, and (2) hypoparathyroidism. title: Explainability-informed patient-disjoint evaluation of deep learning for plus disease in retinopathy of prematurity with an ophthalmologist reader study.
abstract: Background Plus disease is a treatment-relevant sign of retinopathy of prematurity, but fundus images from the same infant may differ in image quality, posterior-pole coverage, and visible vascular severity. We evaluated deep-learning classification using a patient-disjoint design, within-infant variability, and an ophthalmologist reader study. Methods The primary analysis included 732 Phoenix ICON fundus images from 38 infants, assigned exclusively to a 634-image development pool or a 98-image hold-out set from eight previously unseen infants. Five pretrained convolutional neural networks were evaluated at the image level. Hold-out predictions were grouped by infant and laterality to characterize descriptive within-infant variation. A historical secondary analysis used a random image-level partition without enforced patient separation and was considered exploratory. Two ophthalmologists independently graded 30 unique isolated images for inter-observer analysis; 10 were presented twice, resulting in 40 presentations for intra-observer repeatability. Results DenseNet121 achieved an image-level ROC-AUC of 0.929; however, infant-equal-weighted image-level ROC-AUC was 0.905 and leave-one-infant-out ROC-AUC ranged from 0.838 to 0.989, demonstrating sensitivity to the small clustered hold-out cohort. At a development-defined threshold of 0.0184, sensitivity increased to 98.0%, while specificity decreased to 46.8%. Within-infant probability variability was observed across all five CNN architectures. Ophthalmologists 1 and 2 assessed 14/18 and 17/18 plus-reference images, respectively, as Healthy. Exact three-category inter-observer agreement was 26/30 (86.7%), and both reproduced the same severity grade for all 10 repeated images. Conclusions Patient-disjoint evaluation revealed substantial uncertainty in image-level performance and variability among images from the same infant. Cluster-aware analyses showed dependence on the small hold-out cohort, while the development-defined operating point demonstrated a marked sensitivity-specificity trade-off. The reader study showed that an examination-derived reference label and the diagnostic evidence visible in an isolated image are not equivalent, despite high inter-observer agreement and complete categorical repeatability. Because examination identifiers were unavailable, within-infant analyses were interpreted descriptively and not as infant or examination-level diagnostic performance. Clinically useful systems should assess image quality, select informative views, and integrate evidence across multiple images and both eyes. External prospective multicentre validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Evolution of deep learning for structural magnetic resonance imaging analysis in Alzheimer's disease: from slice-level classification to brain structure modeling.
abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) depicts Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related atrophy noninvasively and has become a common input for deep-learning studies of diagnosis and progression. For this structured narrative Mini Review, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, the Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore through 31 August 2026. We then purposively selected recent studies that were informative about model design or evaluation. The review covers two-dimensional convolutional neural networks, three-dimensional and hybrid volumetric architectures, transformers, and foundation models, together with longitudinal, multimodal, and graph-based extensions. Across these approaches, validity depends on clinically meaningful target labels, preprocessing that excludes test-set information, participant-level data separation, and evaluation beyond discrimination. Two-dimensional methods remain useful when data or computing resources are limited, although they do not preserve continuous whole-volume context. Three-dimensional and hybrid models incorporate more volumetric information, but anatomical fidelity still depends on representation and validation. Current AD-specific studies do not show that transformers or foundation models consistently outperform convolutional or hybrid alternatives. Stronger clinical evidence will require external testing, calibrated and uncertainty-aware predictions, transparent reporting, and prospective assessment within the intended workflow.

title: Lymphoma-associated pancreatitis: a multicenter retrospective cohort study with a prediction model.
abstract: Purpose Pancreatitis in patients with hematologic malignancies, particularly lymphoma, is a challenging complication with heterogeneous etiologies. Large studies with systematic etiological classification and prognostic models are lacking. Methods This retrospective multicenter study (2020-2025) included patients with hematologic malignancies who developed acute pancreatitis. Etiologies were adjudicated using predefined criteria. A nomogram-based prediction model was developed with internal bootstrap validation. Results Among 1,705 patients, 31 (1.82%) developed pancreatitis: 19 lymphoma (61.3%), 9 leukemia (29.0%), and 3 plasma cell disorders (9.7%). In the lymphoma cohort (median age 59 years, 57.9% male), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (47.4%) and peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) (21.1%) were most common. Etiology distribution: treatment-related (36.8%), direct pancreatic infiltration (31.6%), conventional (15.8%), multifactorial (10.5%), and infection-related (5.3%). Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided tissue acquisition had 83.3% diagnostic sensitivity for direct infiltration; positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET-CT) showed a "tetrad sign" in 5/6 cases. Severe pancreatitis occurred in 21.1% of lymphoma-associated pancreatitis. The nomogram (incorporating time to pancreatitis ≤30 days, recent L-asparaginase (LAsp)/immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) exposure, and absence of pancreatic mass) discriminated treatment-related from non-treatment-related etiologies with AUC 0.84 (95% CI 0.71-0.96). PTCL subtype (HR 3.12, 95% CI 1.28-7.61, p=0.012), multifactorial etiology (HR 2.56, 95% CI 1.02-6.42, p=0.045), and age ≥65 years (HR 2.01, 95% CI 0.95-4.25, p=0.07) predicted 1-year mortality (C-index 0.79). Summary Lymphoma-associated pancreatitis is rare (1.8% of hematologic malignancies). Treatment-related causes slightly outnumber direct infiltration. EUS-guided tissue acquisition and PET-CT are valuable for differential diagnosis. The nomogram may assist etiological classification and risk stratification, but prospective validation is required.

title: Case Report: Metastatic duodenal hepatoid adenocarcinoma: a rare pathology with exceptional response to dual immune checkpoint blockade.
abstract: Hepatoid adenocarcinoma (HAC) is a rare, malignant, extrahepatic tumor with hepatocellular differentiation. HAC is often associated with elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) concentrations, which makes it difficult to distinguish from primary hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It is a difficult diagnosis based on histopathology, as the immunohistochemistry (IHC) profile often overlaps with hepatocellular carcinoma. HAC can arise from multiple organs, including the stomach, esophagus, colon, pancreas, duodenum, and peritoneum, with the stomach being the most common site. The treatment of HAC is not well defined, as randomized trial data is not available. The overall prognosis of metastatic HAC with standard combination chemotherapy is extremely poor. Here, we present a case of metastatic duodenal HAC that achieved a sustained complete response to chemotherapy-free dual immune checkpoint blockade, which, to our knowledge, represents the first published report of a sustained complete response to chemotherapy-free dual immune checkpoint blockade in metastatic duodenal HAC and suggests a potential approach that warrants further clinical investigation. We acknowledge that a degree of diagnostic uncertainty remains, as HAC and HCC can exhibit essentially identical morphologic and immunophenotypic features, making the distinction largely clinical.

title: A novel multimodal model integrating CT-based deep learning and clinical information for predicting 1-year OS of first-line immunotherapy in ES-SCLC patients.
abstract: Background Extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) is a rare yet highly aggressive malignancy with severely limited treatment options. The efficacy of immunotherapy for ES-SCLC remain limited, with only 14% of patients deriving additional benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), underscoring significant heterogeneity in patient response. This study aimed to develop a model for the accurate prediction of prognosis and therapeutic response to optimize treatment strategies. Methods 99 and 25 ES-SCLC patients were enrolled as training and independent internal validation cohorts. Baseline CT images, clinical data, and laboratory markers were collected. Prognostic factors were screened via Cox regression. A mediastinal window CT-based deep learning model (MWDL) was developed and combined with Progastrin-releasing peptide (log(ProGRP + 1)) and bone metastasis to establish the novel MWGB-Cox model. Results ProGRP and bone metastasis were independent prognostic factors with area under the curves (AUCs) of 0.705 and 0.666 respectively for predicting 1-year OS. Among the pure deep learning models, the MWDL model achieved better performance with a mean AUC of 0.813 than the deep learning model based on lung window CT images (LWDL, AUC 0.756). Whereas the multimodal MWGB-Cox model not only achieved the highest AUC (0.902) for 1-year OS prediction, but also effectively overcame the limitation of insufficient sensitivity. The predictive performance of the MWGB-Cox model was further validated in the independent internal validation cohort. Conclusions This novel, simple, and cost-effective multimodal MWGB-Cox model integrating CT-based deep learning, log(ProGRP + 1), and bone metastasis could robustly predict 1-year OS of ES-SCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, providing a reliable tool for clinical decision-making. Significance By integrating CT-based deep learning, log(ProGRP + 1) levels, and bone metastasis, the novel multimodal model achieved the highest predictive AUC (0.902) with improved sensitivity, serving as a simple, cost-effective tool for clinical decision-making.

title: Case Report: Definitive radiotherapy for intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation.
abstract: Intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma (ITTC) with neuroendocrine differentiation is rare, and evidence for definitive radiotherapy in nonsurgical patients remains limited. A 70-year-old woman with a 1-year history of a neck mass and hoarseness was diagnosed with ITTC with neuroendocrine differentiation based on histopathological, immunohistochemical, and imaging findings. After declining surgery and systemic chemotherapy, she received definitive radiotherapy: 60 Gy in 30 fractions to the planning target volume, followed by a sequential boost of 6 Gy in 3 fractions to the gross primary tumor and involved lymph nodes, for a cumulative dose of 66 Gy in 33 fractions. No grade ≥3 acute treatment-related toxicities occurred. At approximately 2 months after radiotherapy, the sum of target-lesion diameters decreased from 54 mm to 42 mm, a 22.2% reduction. With no new lesions or unequivocal progression of non-target disease, the overall response was classified as stable disease according to RECIST 1.1. This case documents early radiographic tumor reduction following definitive radiotherapy for ITTC, although longer follow-up is required to assess the durability of disease control and late toxicity.

title: Clinical outcomes after reirradiation with dose painting of recurrent or second primary head and neck cancer.
abstract: Purpose Recurrent or second primary head and neck cancer (rsHNC) presents a radiotherapeutic challenge due to limited tolerance of previously irradiated tissues. These patients could benefit from dose painting (DP), which focuses on delivering maximal dose to areas of high tumor burden while respecting dose constraints to organs at risk. In this study, we compare clinical outcomes in one group receiving standard reirradiation with a group receiving 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT-guided DP. Methods Our standard reirradiation regimen is hyperfractionated radiotherapy (RT) of 1.5 Gy x 40 (60 Gy total dose). For DP, we defined two FDG-based prescription volumes receiving at least 65 Gy and 70 Gy. Thirteen patients receiving standard RT were compared with 10 DP patients. Toxicity was scored using CTCAE v3.0. Disease-related endpoints were locoregional control (LRC), disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS). Results The mean composite toxicity score was maximal at the end of RT, with varying patterns across the CTCAE items. No significant difference in toxicity was found between the groups except for dysphagia at 6 months, where the standard RT group had worse scores (p=0.01). No differences were found in LRC and DFS. Two-year OS was 50% in the DP group versus 15% in the standard group (p=0.04), although this may reflect higher comorbidity in the standard group. Conclusion DP of rsHNC did not increase toxicity compared with standard reirradiation. No evidence of improved disease control was found. However, DP may benefit selected patients, and future studies should focus on identifying these candidates. Clinical trial registration https://clinicaltrials.gov, identifier NCT02921581.

title: A biopsy-validated study of combined DL-upscaled MRSI and (18F)-FACBC PET for presurgical glioma diagnosis.
abstract: Medical imaging is crucial for glioma management. Combined with MRI, amino acid PET may improve glioma diagnosis, biopsy targeting, and tumor delineation compared to structural MRI alone. Magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) complements both structural MRI and PET by detecting metabolites such as N-acetylaspartate (NAA), creatine (Cr), and choline (Cho), which are markers for brain health and tumor malignancy, but is challenged by low spatial resolution. This study evaluates whether upscaled MRSI enhanced by deep learning can improve diagnostic accuracy and serve as a complement or alternative to PET for glioma classification. Ten glioma patients (ages 24-80) were included. Presurgical [18F]-FACBC PET/MRI, including proton 2D MRSI, was acquired for all patients. Thirty-two image-guided biopsies were sampled during surgery from the patients and classified as glioma tissue or non-tumor tissue, and according to IDH1 status. For each biopsy location, tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) and standardized uptake value (SUV) from PET, and tCho/NAA and tCho/tCr ratios from MRSI were calculated. ROC analysis was used to assess the accuracy of [18F]-FACBC PET and upscaled MRSI, and the combinations of these in classifying glioma vs non-tumor tissue and IDH1 status. Among the individual biomarkers evaluated, the tCho/NAA ratio from the deep learning-based model demonstrated the highest apparent AUC for classifying glioma vs. non-tumor tissue (AUC = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.66-1.0), compared with tCho/tCr (AUC = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.54-1:00), SUV (AUC = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.49-0.90), and TBR (AUC = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.48-0.86). Combining TBR with tCho/NAA and/or tCho/tCr improved tissue classification compared to either modality alone, where TBR+tCho/NAA+tCho/tCr showed the best results (AUC = 0.91, 95% CI: 0.71-1.0). MRSI was a poor predictor for IDH1 -status (tCho/NAA: AUC = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.44-0.88 and tCho/tCr: AUC = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.17-0.60), while PET was an excellent predictor (SUV: AUC = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.66-0.95 and TBR: AUC = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.65-0.94) and the combination of SUV, tCho/NAA, and tCho/tCr was a best predictor (AUC = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.88-1.0). Combining DL-upscaled MRSI with [18F]-FACBC PET appeared to enhance discrimination between glioma and non-tumor tissue, a finding that warrants validation in larger, prospective studies.

title: Case Report: Pyrrolizidine alkaloid-induced hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome misdiagnosed as ovarian malignancy.
abstract: Background Hepatic Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome (HSOS), formerly known as Hepatic Veno-Occlusive Disease (HVOD), is a rare and life-threatening liver condition. It is often caused by the ingestion of pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs), which are found in plants such as Gynura segetum (Tusanqi). Because its clinical presentation is non-specific, HSOS is frequently misdiagnosed. Case presentation A 72-year-old female with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes presented with abdominal distension and anorexia for 2 weeks. Initial examinations revealed massive ascites and significantly elevated tumor markers (Cancer Antigen 125(CA125): 195.0 U/mL, Human Epididymis Protein 4(HE4): 120.1 pmol/L). Imaging suggested potential ovarian cancer, leading to diagnostic laparoscopy and bilateral adnexectomy. However, intraoperative findings and post-operative pathology showed no evidence of malignancy, identifying only a serous cystadenoma. Subsequent detailed history-taking revealed long-term ingestion of "Tusanqi." Re-evaluation via contrast-enhanced CT and MRCP showed characteristic patterns: patchy enhancement of hepatic parenchyma ("geographic" pattern), narrow hepatic veins, and signs of portal hypertension. The patient was finally diagnosed with PA-induced HSOS. Following a regimen of anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin), liver protection, and diuretics, the patient's abdominal distension relieved, and liver function markers showed partial recovery. The patient underwent laparoscopic bilateral adnexectomy due to a high suspicion of ovarian cancer, but the postoperative pathology ruled out malignant tumors, resulting in unnecessary surgical trauma. This article aims to improve the warning effect. Conclusion This case highlights the clinical challenge of distinguishing HSOS from abdominal malignancies. A thorough dietary/herbal history and characteristic "geographic" enhancement on imaging are pivotal for avoiding unnecessary surgical interventions.

title: Prior-Enhanced Axial TransUNet: integrating MedSAM priors and sparse region-aware attention for kidney-tumor segmentation.
abstract: Accurate kidney and renal-tumor segmentation is challenging because lesion size, location, morphology, and boundary contrast vary substantially across abdominal CT scans. Most existing methods rely on a single form of local evidence and struggle to recover the boundaries of small lesions while maintaining global anatomical consistency. This paper proposes Prior-Enhanced Axial TransUNet (PEAT), which combines the broad medical representations of foundation models with task-specific discriminative learning. PEAT introduces three core components: Bottleneck Semantic Alignment (BSA) uses the frozen MedSAM image encoder as a training-stage feature reference and guides the semantic organization of the task network's bottleneck representation through an L1 alignment constraint; Dual-path Attention-enhanced Fusion (DAF) adaptively fuses CNN local features with MaxViT global contextual features by cascading coordinate attention and SENetV2; and Bi-granular Region-Aware Attention (BRA) achieves efficient non-local context modeling through Top- k window routing and patch-level sparse interaction. The MedSAM branch participates only during training, and only the task-specific network runs at inference. Under a setting in which all compared methods adopt the same preprocessing and evaluation protocol, PEAT achieves kidney and tumor Dice scores of 97.69% and 91.83% on KiTS21 and 96.80% and 92.58% on KiTS23, respectively. Across all four tasks, PEAT attains the highest Dice among the compared methods; ablation studies further show that the progressive integration of BSA, DAF, and BRA yields consistent gains, with the complete model outperforming all single and pairwise configurations. These results indicate that combining training-stage broad feature guidance with task-specific representation learning effectively improves kidney and renal-tumor segmentation and provides a viable route for the coordinated design of foundation-model priors and lightweight task networks.
